detail.abstract: The focus on the subject of intelligence has recently gained ground, particularly because of concerns regarding artficial intelligence (AI) replacing natural intelligence (NI). Developers of AI have different agendas, and have been encouraged to be ethical in their pursuits. In core, ethical AI development is aimed at ensuring the safety of humanity. Educational institutions are currently restructing their courses in an attempt not to produce obsolete graduates. However, in the realm of intelligence, there is one form of intelligence that is beyond scientific understanding, and this is supernatural intelligence (SI). Essentially, SI is the foundation of the other two forms of intelligence. Thus, a thorough understanding of the relationships among these forms of intelligence becomes non-negotiable, particularly in relation to the achievement of development goals. The 2015 transition from Millenium Development Goals (MDGs) to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), signalled the need to further achieve certain key development goals. The current concerns surrounding ethical AI development could be addressed by linking AI development to specific SDGs. Consequently, the main objectives of this study were to 1) interrogate the connectedness of the three forms of intelligence, thereby mapping out a way for effective collaboration among these forms of intelligence; and to elaborate how AI can foster the achievement of SDGs. To achieve the above, a desktop literature review was used. From the comparisons conducted, it was found that supernatural intelligence is on top, followed by natural intelligence, and finally artficial intelligence. Furthermore, if properly aligned, these forms of intelligence have been found to have the capability to positively impact the societies through the speedy achievement of SDGs.

title: We are all Betting (Serving) -Thee Unravelling of Thee Ugly Truth: An Investigative Literature Review
affiliations: Mirracle Consultants

detail.title: We are all Betting (Serving) -Thee Unravelling of Thee Ugly Truth: An Investigative Literature Review
detail.abstract: In the present day world, people involved in betting activities are looked upon with disdain, especially in religious circles. However, an introspection into the terminology used in the betting industry, suggests strong connectedness between betting activities and uplifted societal norms. An example of the present day dilemma is the uplifting of forex and/or crypto traders and the shunning of Aviator pilots (panthers) which are merely uncertified photocopies of traders. In an attempt to clear the mist surrounding this and other misconceptions, this confirmatory study was conducted with an aim to reveal the hidden connectedness of betting activities and acceptable societal norms. To accomplish the main aim of this confirmatory study, inspiration and an investigative non-empirical approach, in the form of literature review were utilised. The literature review process was conducted in accordance to the PRISMA framework. From the findings, it was confirmed, beyond reasonable doubt, that Aviator game and forex/crypto trading are two sides of the same coin. The results also revealed that employment (formalised slavery) and education are essentially betting activities that have been formalised and given official names. Ultimately, it was concluded that having a funeral policy is the only activity that is divergent from betting.

title: The Imported Mismatch Rule in Light of the Fundamental Freedoms
affiliations: Aalto, Business Law

detail.title: The Imported Mismatch Rule in Light of the Fundamental Freedoms
detail.abstract: This article analyses the imported mismatch rule contained in Article 9(3) of the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD) from the perspective of the fundamental freedoms. At the core of the analysis stands the insight that intra-EU payments can trigger the national implementation of the imported mismatch rule. This is not what the drafters of Action 2 of the OECD/G20 Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) project Action 2 and, thereupon, Article 9 of the ATAD wanted to see. Yet, it became possible due to Member States not applying the anti-hybrid mismatch rules consistently.

title: Playing Aviator Like a Forex Trader using Patience of a Retailer: Thee Rise of Professional Aviator Pilots in Africa (PAPA)
affiliations: Mirracle Consultants

detail.title: Playing Aviator Like a Forex Trader using Patience of a Retailer: Thee Rise of Professional Aviator Pilots in Africa (PAPA)
detail.abstract: The degradation of economies, particularly in Africa, has led many to seek alternative means to survive, popularly known as side hustles. At first, it was network marketing then came trading (forex and crypto); and recently betting has been on the rise. Among the available betting options, Aviator is currently at the apex. While a handful of Aviator "pilots" are winning in the long term, most of them are losing the little that they have in pursuit of instant financial turnaround. While betting is a hobby in other developed continents, most Africans are participating in it for their livelihood. Thus, the main objectives guiding this study were to 1) develop a new theory that is fundamental to the Aviator game, and to 2) develop and present a tested framework that can be used by Aviator Pilots in Africa (APA) to earn a living from a game that is almost a replica of trading. To achieve the above, an empirical research design in the form of action research, observation and autoethnography was used in the study. Furthermore, considering the absence of scholarly literature on this phenomenon, this study was also exploratory ìn nature. Considering the new international poverty line of $3 per person per day, it was found that Aviator has the potential to alleviate poverty challenges in Africa. With regards to its relation to trading, a significant number of similarities were found. Consequently, it was recommended that African businesses, especially in lower middle income countries, should consider investing in developing Professional Aviator Pilots (PAPs) for their businesses.

title: Youth in the Permanent Stream: Digital Media, Self-Regulation, and Societal Responsibility

detail.title: Youth in the Permanent Stream: Digital Media, Self-Regulation, and Societal Responsibility
detail.abstract:
Digital media structure adolescents’ everyday lives with unprecedented intensity. Smartphones enable continuous social connectivity, immediate access to information, and constant stimulation. At the same time, internalizing symptoms such as depressive moods, anxiety, and sleep disturbances have increased across many Western societies.

This paper integrates meta-analyses, longitudinal studies, and developmental neuroscience to examine how digital media use relates to self-regulation, emotional processing, and identity development. Findings indicate small but consistent associations between intensive, particularly passive, social media use and depressive symptoms, attentional difficulties, sleep problems, and reduced self-esteem, moderated by usage patterns, emotional motives, attachment quality, and contextual factors.

The central argument is that developmental risk arises not from digital media per se, but from the interaction of permanent stimulus availability, algorithmically reinforced attention capture, and still-maturing self-regulatory capacities during adolescence. The paper advances a societal responsibility perspective, emphasizing relational guidance, structural safeguards, and intentional design of digital environments. It aims to move beyond alarmism and trivialization, offering a psychologically grounded framework for prevention, education, and policy.

title: Determinants of Stock Market Correlations: Accounting for Model Uncertainty and Reverse Causality in a Large Panel Setting
affiliations: ISEG, Universidade de Lisboa, Lazarski University and University of Westminster

detail.title: Determinants of Stock Market Correlations: Accounting for Model Uncertainty and Reverse Causality in a Large Panel Setting

declarations.ethicsApproval: Do not apply

detail.abstract: We examine 22 determinants of stock market correlations in a panel setting with 651 country pairs of developed economies over 2001-2018, while accounting for model uncertainty and reverse causality. This robust empirical approach and the consideration of a broad range of factors provides the following key findings: (i) inertia, market size and interconnected financial factors such as capital mobility, financial development and portfolio equity flows are all important in explaining the degree of correlation of stock market returns (ii) a number of determinants, well established in the literature, e.g. trade, institutional distance, and exchange rate volatility were not able to withstand a rigorous accounting for model uncertainty within the Bayesian model averaging framework. In sum, given the expected future growth of economies and their capital markets, as well as deepening financial liberalization, this paper strongly supports the hypothesis of diminishing international diversification potential.

title: District Heterogeneity, Legislative Bargaining, and Trade Policy
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin, University of Houston and Research Economist

detail.title: District Heterogeneity, Legislative Bargaining, and Trade Policy

publicationDetails.detailsText: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Working Papers, volume 26, issue 04, 2026[10.21144/wp26-04]

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The diverse economic structures of Congressional Districts generate heterogeneous trade policy preferences. The crucial role of these district-level interests in determining trade policy in Congress is largely absent from canonical political economy models of trade (e.g. Grossman and Helpman, 1994). We address this gap by modeling the aggregation of district preferences into national trade policy through legislative bargaining. This supply-side explanation of trade policy builds on the legislative bargaining framework of Baron and Ferejohn (1989) and Celik, Karabay and McLaren (2013). The model yields a unified account of trade policy formation in which institutional design, economic and political geography, and bargaining in the presence of an agenda setter jointly determine the equilibrium level of protection.

title: Game Theory of the "Three Red Lines" and Earnings Manipulation - Signal Jamming and the Formation of Off-Balance Sheet Debt in the Chinese Real Estate Market
affiliations: Rodem Asset Co.,Ltd. CEO

detail.title: Game Theory of the "Three Red Lines" and Earnings Manipulation - Signal Jamming and the Formation of Off-Balance Sheet Debt in the Chinese Real Estate Market
detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the mechanism by which the "Three Red Lines" financing regulations, introduced by the Chinese government in 2020, unintentionally rendered developer financial risks invisible. By applying the "Signal Jamming" model from corporate finance theory, we elucidate the following paradox: strict quantitative regulations (the Red Lines) provided developers with strong incentives to manipulate apparent financial figures using high-cost "off-balance sheet debt" (such as shadow banking and "Equity in name, Debt in reality" schemes). In equilibrium, although the market (banks and regulators) anticipates the manipulation and discounts the figures accordingly, developers fall into a prisoner's dilemma where they "must manipulate or be deemed inferior." Consequently, they continue to falsify data while incurring costs that destroy social welfare. This analysis suggests that quantitative regulations lacking informational transparency can conversely increase systemic risk.

title: The Demography of Progress: A Multi-Disciplinary Analysis of Population-Centric Development Models and the Calculus of Global Equity
affiliations: Independant

detail.title: The Demography of Progress: A Multi-Disciplinary Analysis of Population-Centric Development Models and the Calculus of Global Equity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No
declarations.ethicsApproval: Yes
declarations.funderStatement: No

detail.abstract:
The fundamental paradigm of contemporary developmental theory, the unbreakable connection between global resource allocation and human population metrics is examined in this paper. While territorial sovereignty is frequently emphasized in traditional geopolitical models, "Per Capita" and "Density-Dependent" metrics are becoming more and more central to modern development frameworks developed by the World Bank, IMF, and UN.

A three-pronged analytical framework is used in this study to explain this phenomenon. It starts by looking at agglomeration economics and showing how labor density multiplies capital and technological output using the Solow-Swan Growth Model. Second, it examines the biopolitics of public health, where the "Global Burden of Disease" (GBD) and "Disability-Adjusted Life Years" (DALY) require that medical infrastructure attain statistical efficacy by tracking the highest concentration of human life. Third, it challenges the Infrastructure-Density Correlation, emphasizing the "Last Mile" paradox, which states that in sparse areas, the marginal cost of connectivity frequently outweighs the total social benefit.

The paper further analyzes the transition into the "Digital Frontier," where the rise of biometric identity (ID4D) and mobile penetration has shifted the development focus from physical geography to "Digital Populations. The study comes to the conclusion that population-based models are mathematically inevitable due to the need to strike a balance between democratic legitimacy and fiscal efficiency. However, it cautions that this "majoritarian" approach requires integrated "safety-net" sub-models to prevent the systematic marginalization of ultra-rural and indigenous populations.

title: Central Bank Collateral Policy and the Allocation of Safe Assets in Secured Funding Markets
affiliations: Deutsche Bundesbank and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: Central Bank Collateral Policy and the Allocation of Safe Assets in Secured Funding Markets
detail.abstract: We show that central bank collateral policy affects the allocation and pricing of collateral in secured funding markets. For identification we take advantage of a temporary extension of the European Central Bank's collateral framework that allowed banks to pledge previously ineligible credit claims for refinancing. Using a difference-indifferences design based on banks' ex-ante collateral composition, we find that banks affected by the temporary extension substitute away from government bonds in central bank operations and instead redeploy these assets as collateral in the repo market, leading to higher lending volumes, greater collateral reuse, lower repo specialness and rate dispersion. Our findings thus demonstrate that collateral framework design influences the effective supply and distribution of collateral in secured funding markets.

title: Global Knowledge Flows in High-Tech Sectors: Evidence from Patents
affiliations: Department of Economics, Suffolk University and Suffolk University

detail.title: Global Knowledge Flows in High-Tech Sectors: Evidence from Patents
detail.abstract: This study examines international knowledge flows in self-driving, electric vehicle, and semiconductor technologies using global patent data from 2010 to 2024. Chinese patenting grew rapidly, making China the largest contributor in these sectors. Despite this growth in patenting volume, a large share of influential patents continue to originate from firms headquartered in the United States, Japan, Germany, and South Korea. Across all three technologies, Chinese inventors receive relatively fewer citations from foreign inventors, indicating limited global diffusion of Chinese-origin knowledge. In contrast, patents from the United States and Japan are widely cited across countries, consistent with their role as central sources of globally-diffused knowledge. After 2018, following trade tensions between the U.S. and China, bilateral knowledge exchange increased, particularly through the intangible knowledge embedded in patents. Overall, the evidence indicates that the two countries increasingly rely on each other's intangible knowledge rather than physical technologies.

title: Effectiveness of Climate Policy Instruments in India's Building Sector
affiliations: Tyche Investments - Climate Consulting Group

detail.title: Effectiveness of Climate Policy Instruments in India's Building Sector
detail.abstract:
India's building sector, accounting for approximately 30% of energy consumption and projected to quintuple by 2050, presents both a significant climate challenge and mitigation opportunity. The government has implemented regulatory (ECBC, ENS), economic (PAT scheme), and informational and voluntary (GRIHA, LEED, BEE labelling) policy instruments, yet questions persist regarding their actual effectiveness.

To systematically evaluate the effectiveness of climate policy instruments implemented by Indian Central and State Governments in the built environment in reducing greenhouse gas emissions compared to baseline scenarios over 2005–2025. A systematic literature review following PRISMA guidelines was conducted across Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar. Narrative synthesis was employed with findings stratified by policy type and baseline assumptions.

The findings suggests that regulatory instruments (ECBC, ENS) demonstrate 30–50% potential energy savings, yet actual reductions remain far lower due to weak enforcement and limited state adoption. The PAT scheme achieves cost-effective 5–8% savings above baseline with negative abatement costs. GRIHA-rated buildings show 30–50% lower energy consumption but represent <0.1% of building stock. Critically, 30–40% of projected reductions would occur without dedicated policies due to autonomous technological progress. Embodied carbon (40–50% of emissions by 2050) and the informal sector (30–40% of stock) remain entirely unaddressed.

India has the policies; what remains inadequate is their implementation. Strengthening enforcement, expanding scope to embodied carbon and informal sector, developing data systems, and designing integrated policy packages are urgently needed to bridge the implementation gap.

title: The Care Economy and Macroeconomic Outcomes: A Structuralist Approach
affiliations: New School for Social Research

detail.title: The Care Economy and Macroeconomic Outcomes: A Structuralist Approach

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A

detail.abstract: Inspired by feminist macroeconomics, this paper shows how a Marx-Keynes-Schumpeter (MKS) macrodynamic system can be augmented by simple models of the care economy. To this end, an MKS model of steady-state growth and distribution is extended to include: first, a model of unpaid domestic care-giving within the household; and second, a model of household acquisition of marketed care services. It is shown that the care economy affects basic macroeconomic outcomes, such as labour productivity, aggregate demand formation, and the steady-state growth rate. The chief conclusion is that the care economy should be the subject of more routine attention in macroeconomic theory.

title: The Implementation of the Basel Capital Accord in Brazil
affiliations: GODKE ADVOGADOS

detail.title: The Implementation of the Basel Capital Accord in Brazil
detail.abstract: This paper examines how prudential regulation—particularly the Basel Committee’s capital-adequacy framework—responds to the transition from the post–World War II era of relatively stable, protected banking systems to the late-twentieth-century environment of intensified competition, financial innovation, and recurring bank distress. Against this backdrop, the study analyzes Brazil’s domestic implementation of the 1988 Basel Capital Accord (Basel I), adopted in Brazil in 1994, and evaluates the regulatory, legal, and economic consequences of that implementation. It then assesses the policy rationale and design choices embedded in the then-proposed “New Capital Accord” (Basel II), with particular attention to its risk-sensitivity and the practical challenges it raises for supervisory authorities and regulated institutions. Building on a survey of Brazil’s financial-system architecture and applicable regulatory measures, the paper offers a critical appraisal of the Basel I framework as implemented in Brazil—highlighting operational frictions, incentive effects, and points of legal and economic tension—and uses these findings to frame the prospects for a more effective domestic adoption of Basel II. The concluding chapter advances policy recommendations aimed at improving the quality of implementation, strengthening supervisory outcomes, and reducing volatility without unduly constraining financial intermediation.

title: On-Location vs Online Platform Work: Job Quality and Mental Wellbeing across Europe
affiliations: University of Warwick, , Universitat Pompeu Fabra (UPF), Karolinska Institutet - Institute of Environmental Medicine, , University of Copenhagen, University of Copenhagen - Copenhagen University, , Tampere University, , University of Lodz, , , , University of Lodz, Tampere University, University of Lodz, , Universitat Pompeu Fabra (UPF), Universitat Pompeu Fabra (UPF) and

The views expressed in this article are solely those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of the funding bodies.

detail.abstract: This study examines platform work across seven European countries, investigating job quality and mental wellbeing outcomes. Applying a multidimensional job quality framework to survey data from the UK, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, Poland, Spain and Sweden, we find systematic differences in job quality by type of platform work (on-location and online) and country. Our analysis reveals consistent disparities in Physical Environment and Work Intensity, with online workers experiencing more favourable conditions, while other job quality dimensions, e.g., Earnings, Contract Types, Social Environment, Autonomy and Working Time Quality, vary by national context. Crucially, platform work type shows no significant direct association with mental wellbeing. Instead, job quality dimensions, particularly Social Environment, Working Time Quality and Work Intensity, emerge as the pivotal determinants of platform workers' mental wellbeing. These findings challenge homogeneous conceptualisations of platform work, demonstrating that mental wellbeing disparities among platform workers operate through specific job quality mechanisms shaped by the interplay between type of platform work and national institutional framework. In doing so, the study highlights the value of job quality as an analytical lens for understanding mental wellbeing outcomes in platform work and informing context-sensitive policy development.

title: Leveraging Diversity for Privileged Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation for Facial Expression Recognition
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Leveraging Diversity for Privileged Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation for Facial Expression Recognition
detail.abstract: Learning privileged information allows a model to exploit data from additional modalities only available during training. State-of-the-art methods for privileged knowledge distillation (PKD) have been proposed to distill information from a teacher model (that combines different prevalent and privileged modalities) to a student model (without access to privileged modalities). Recently, methods have been proposed to capture and distill the structural information and outperform point-to-point PKD methods. However such PKD methods are primarily confined to learning from a single joint teacher representation, which limits their robustness, accuracy, and ability to learn from diverse sources. Diversity in the feature space leads to higher performance in such a distillation scheme. This paper proposes multi-teacher privileged knowledge distillation, a novel method for diversifying the teacher space by recycling the existing backbone feature representations and aligning them with the multimodal space using lightweight adaptation. A simple yet effective teacher selection mechanism implicitly mitigates the negative transfer and allows distillation from the most accurate teacher at each distillation step. The MT-PKDOT employs a structural similarity KD mechanism based on entropy regularized optimal transport for distillation. An additional constraint is added to the loss function to explicitly align the centroids in the student space. The proposed MT-PKDOT method was validated on Affwild2 and Biovid databases. Results indicate that our proposed method is able to improve over the existing state-of-the-art privileged knowledge distillation methods, and in cases where the alignment is ineffective, MTPKDOT is able to maintain the performance similar to single-teacher methods. It improves the visual-only baseline on the Biovid dataset by 5.8%. On the Affwild2 dataset, the proposed method improves 4% and 5% over the visual-only lower bound for valence and arousal, respectively.The code is made publicly available at: https://github.com/haseebaslam95/MT-PKDOT.

title: Capital Is King - Leveraging Crowdfunding in Trading and Aviator: A Literature Review
affiliations: Mirracle Consultants

detail.title: Capital Is King - Leveraging Crowdfunding in Trading and Aviator: A Literature Review
detail.abstract: Millions of people, particularly in developing countries, are losing money on a daily basis to forex and crypto trading, and recently to Aviator. Various reasons have been cited for this appalling situation, and lack of capital is among the most prevalent reasons. Although these seemingly lucrative options have claimed lives of many, many people are still hoping their financial situations will be positively turned by them. Thus, the aim of this study was to raise awareness with regards to the power of crowdfunding, in relation to trading and Aviator. To achieve the above, a systematic literature review was conducted. From the results, it was affirmed that indeed crowdfunding, coupled with financial prudence, has the potential to positively impact the masses of people in developing countries. Furthermore, it was noted that combining crowdfunding and the novel concept of professional aviator pilots in Africa, has the potential to create a sector with significant potential to eradicate poverty and inequality.

title: Procedural Gates and Stage-indexed Feasibility a Formal Specification for Claim-boundedness, Pleading Lock, and Ex Officio Authority

detail.title: Procedural Gates and Stage-indexed Feasibility a Formal Specification for Claim-boundedness, Pleading Lock, and Ex Officio Authority
detail.abstract: This paper models adjudication not as unconstrained deduction from substantive norms, but as a procedurally bounded search space. Bridging normative-systems theory and computational law, this work provides a rigorous formal specification in which procedural rules act as typed set-transformers (gates) over decision dimensions. Explicit operators are defined for three procedural primitives: a claim-boundedness gate (G claim), a stage-indexed pleading-lock gate (G lock), and a rigorously formulated evidence-processing gate (G ev) whose internal consequence relation is explicitly typed. Procedural Hallucination is anchored within the deontic derogation-gap literature (Alchourrón and Bulygin 1971; Navarro and Rodríguez 2014), formalizing it as the computational manifestation of the 'permitted but infeasible' configuration in an AI agent. Two theorems are proved: (T1) a strengthened Monotonicity of Pleading Lock covering both full and partial updates, establishing that D feasible (s) is non-increasing in the relief dimension under any partial denial by G lock ; and (T2) a non-circular Dimensional Isolation theorem whose proof proceeds by independence of gate domains rather than by definitional substitution. A genuinely non-trivial derivation-the dual-lock deadlock, where both the qualification and the relief ceiling are locked at different stages-demonstrates a system failure mode that practitioner intuition does not reliably predict. Strict verification criteria derived from the theorems provide a certifiable architecture for procedurally sound legal decision-support systems.

title: Transformative Competition Law
affiliations: University of Warsaw, Faculty of Management and The University of Manchester

detail.title: Transformative Competition Law
detail.abstract: The article sets competition law in the transformative context. It explains that competition law is not only something that is transformed, but that is transformative in its own right. A twofold argument is advanced: first, that competition law has an important role to play in ensuring that the wide range of transitions in play today (i.e. green, digital and industrial) are both just and enduring, and second, that there are significant lessons to be learnt from economic transformations that have already taken place in Central and Eastern European (CEE) countries and countries from the Global South. To this end, the article explains that the manner in which CEE and selected Global South countries designed and enforced their competition laws allowed competition law to play a meaningful role not only as an instrument but also as an architect of their economic transformations. Against this background, the EU's openness to these transitional experiences is desirable not only because it would supplement the transitions within the EU but also because it will facilitate the pathway to similar transitions in other non-European jurisdictions that look to the EU for guidance. In terms of structure, first, the article examines the role that competition law can play in the course of transitions. Second, it examines the possibilities and limitations of the role competition law has already played in the transitions in CEE and Global South countries. It concludes with an invitation to all readers to engage with the debate on the roles of competition law in a time of transition.

title: Firm Liquidity and the Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations in a Network Economy

detail.title: Firm Liquidity and the Origins of Aggregate Fluctuations in a Network Economy

declarations.funderStatement: I gratefully acknowledge financial support from the University of Essex Social Sciences Doctoral Scholarship.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how microeconomic origins of liquidity shocks at the firm level influence aggregate output and financial stability in a network economy with inter-sectoral linkages. We use firm-level balance sheet data to construct two liquidity measures: the quick ratio, capturing firms' internal short-term liquidity, and a network-based measure, capturing inter-sectoral network structure of liquidity flows derived from receivables and payables. Using sector-level aggregates, we apply a Structural Vector Autoregression (SVAR) model to examine the dynamic responses of GDP, the repo rates, the quick ratio, and the network measure to liquidity shocks. We further decompose forecast error variance to assess the relative contribution of each shock to business-cycle fluctuations. The main results indicate that the network effect is the dominant driver of businesscycle fluctuations, followed by the quick ratio, with both outweighing the remaining endogenous variables. The findings are relevant for macroprudential oversight, highlighting the importance of monitoring firms' liquidity imbalances and network structure for financial stability and economic resilience.

title: Less Innovation, More Religion: Plague's Cultural Imprint in Early-Modern Britain
affiliations: Washington and Lee University - Department of Economics and Department of Economics

detail.title: Less Innovation, More Religion: Plague's Cultural Imprint in Early-Modern Britain
detail.abstract: We empirically examine the plague's impact on print culture in Britain, 1525-1700. Our approach combines yearly data on plague intensity with annual measures of innovativeness (quality) and output volume (quantity). These measures vary across cultural domains and are constructed from a large corpus representative of early-modern British print culture. Plague shocks initially stimulated quality but dampened it over the longer term. By contrast, quantity collapsed after plague outbreaks yet eventually recovered. The plague's lasting imprint on print culture was twofold: a widespread decline in innovativeness across cultural domains and a sustained rise in the volume of religious output.

title: Rising Skill Supply, Technological Changes, and Innovation: A Quantitative Exploration of China
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland and Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE)

detail.title: Rising Skill Supply, Technological Changes, and Innovation: A Quantitative Exploration of China
detail.abstract: Can the expansion of higher education lead to firm productivity growth? In this paper, we examine how China’s college expansion program contributes to the rapid growth of firms’ R&D expenditure and productivity. In our model, heterogeneous firms make endogenous R&D decisions, requiring them to allocate skilled workers between production and R&D. We structurally estimate the model using firm-level data on the level and distribution of R&D, as well as macro-level data on skill prices and sectoral allocation. Quantitative analysis reveals that between 2004 and 2018, the combination of the R&D-sector-biased technology shock, the skill-biased technology shock, and the skilled-labor supply shock leads to a 12 percent increase in total factor productivity (TFP), of which one-fifth is explained by the rising supply of skilled labor. Counterfactual analysis shows that a further increase in the share of skilled labor has the potential to increase TFP by an additional 2 percent, but the marginal effect diminishes due to the rising wages of unskilled labor.

title: Strengthening Water Governance in mining areas through Remote Sensing: A Case Study of Emerlo’s Abandoned Colliery in South Africa
affiliations: and University of the Witwatersrand

detail.title: Strengthening Water Governance in mining areas through Remote Sensing: A Case Study of Emerlo’s Abandoned Colliery in South Africa
detail.abstract: Abandoned coal mines such as the Golfview colliery near Ermelo continue to be a source of environmental and public health risk due to a lack of formal closure and rehabilitation processes. This study evaluated hydrological and water quality impacts of the abandoned Golfview Colliery and explored using a multi-temporal remote sensing approach in governance. Leveraging the Google Earth Engine platform with 430 cloud-free images, a 21-year dataset (2003 to 2024) of Landsat 7/8 and Sentinel-2 imagery was used to analyze the surface water dynamics in the adjacent Douglas and Willem Brummer dams. The Modified Normalized Difference Water Index (MNDWI) was used to quantify surface water extent, and assesed water quality changes using Acid Mine Drainage Index (AMDI), Normalized Difference Turbidity Index (NDTI), and Colored Dissolved Organic Matter (CDOM). Results revealed significant hydrological regime shift following abandonment in 2015. Mean surface water area increased by 30%, indicating groundwater rebound after cessation of dewatering, and a 43.7% increase in the frequency of dry periods, revealing decreased water reliability. The dams had different responses, with Willem Brummer Dam showing a 44.5% increase in area while Douglas Dam remained stable. The indices revealed increasing vegetation cover, elevated turbidity, persistent AMD signatures, and seasonal chlorophyll spikes. This paper recommends the incorporation of remote sensing into South Africa’s water governance frameworks by highlighting its capacity for sustainable means of long-term and cost-effective monitoring. The study aims to contribute towards policy development, encourage more accountable governance practices aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 6, and guiding environmental investment.

title: Beyond crisis response: The selective persistence of crisis-induced innovations in professional audit practice
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, La Trobe University, Faculty of Business, Economics and Law, Students, Monash University, Monash University and Monash University - Monash University Malaysia

detail.title: Beyond crisis response: The selective persistence of crisis-induced innovations in professional audit practice
detail.abstract: This study examines how environmental jolts shape institutional change in professional auditing, arguing that jolts can function not only as opportunity-creators but also as "institutional archaeology" — excavating pre-existing contradictions buried beneath taken-for-granted legitimacy. Drawing on 28 longitudinal interviews with Malaysian Big 4 auditors (2020–2024), we examine why some pandemic-induced audit innovations achieved institutional lock-in while others reverted once restrictions lifted. We find that innovations that persisted addressed problems auditors had long recognised but could not pursue because the logic of material co-presence rendered alternatives illegitimate — resolving tensions that existed before, during, and after the pandemic. Persistence depended on three conditions: resolution of pre-existing practice tensions (C1), multi-stakeholder alignment (C2), and bridging of global-local capability gaps (C3). In our developing-economy context, persistence was predominantly driven by external mandates resolving asymmetries between global standards and local capabilities — a C3-type pathway — rather than by local optimisation driven by actor agency, as characterises advanced-economy studies. This geography-contingent pattern calls into question the implicit universalism of institutional entrepreneurship theory and has practical implications for how global audit firms manage practice consistency across different economic contexts.

title: "Let them Eat Cake" at Mar-a-Lago: Retribution, Revolution, and the Financial Folklore of the Trump Sons
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: "Let them Eat Cake" at Mar-a-Lago: Retribution, Revolution, and the Financial Folklore of the Trump Sons
detail.abstract: This paper examines the rhetorical and ideological dimensions of Eric Trump’s February 2026 dismissal of fixed-income investing as a refuge for those lacking “backbone,” delivered at the World Liberty Forum at Mar-a-Lago. Drawing on the historical parallel of Marie Antoinette’s apocryphal remark, the analysis argues that Trump’s counsel reveals a fundamental conflation of financial capacity with moral character. By framing risk tolerance as a virtue independent of wealth, the rhetoric obscures the asymmetric consequences of investment loss across income strata and exploits the economic concept of marginal utility to serve a populist narrative. The paper further critiques the brothers’ debanking claims and their promotion of World Liberty Financial’s USD1 stablecoin as a vehicle that is structurally dependent upon the very regulated financial infrastructure it purports to replace. The analysis concludes that, far from representing financial courage, the “boring bond” constitutes a rational and defensible instrument of wealth preservation, one whose dismissal reflects the detachment of dynastic privilege rather than any deficiency in its holders.

title: Multidimensional Sustainability Assessment of Local Rice Farming Systems in Indonesia: Evidence from the Rojolele Srinuk Variety
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Multidimensional Sustainability Assessment of Local Rice Farming Systems in Indonesia: Evidence from the Rojolele Srinuk Variety
detail.abstract: The local rice varieties have a significant role in maintaining food security, agricultural biodiversity, and livelihoods in rural Indonesia. Nevertheless, local rice farming systems are under pressure in terms of environmental management, technology adoption, and institutional support. This paper evaluates the sustainability status of the Rojolele Srinuk rice system in Klaten Regency, Indonesia, using a multidimensional framework that integrates the psychosocial, ecological, economic, technological, and institutional dimensions. The data were gathered from various stakeholders and analysed using Multidimensional Scaling (MDS), leverage analysis, and Monte Carlo simulation. The findings reveal that Rojolele Srinuk rice production is moderately sustainable, with a sustainability index of 54.5-59.0 across the five study locations. The psychosocial aspect performs relatively well, especially when agricultural extension services, farming experience, and local knowledge are involved. The performance of the ecological and economic dimensions is moderate, whereas the technological and institutional dimensions are relatively weak due to a lack of mechanisation, marketing technology, and research support. Water and land conservation, farming income, marketing technology, and research support have been identified as sustainability drivers through leverage analysis. These results indicate a need to reinforce the use of technology and institutional alignment to improve the sustainability of local rice farming systems in the long term and to support food security policies in Indonesia.

title: Natural capital: the boom and bust of a metaphor?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Natural capital: the boom and bust of a metaphor?
detail.abstract: Despite a fifty-year academic history, the concept of ’natural capital’ has only been translated into national policy and practice more recently. Since the early 2000s, global initiatives like The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity and the UN System for Environmental Economic Accounts have spurred country-level adoption of natural capital approaches around the world. To examine the implications of this uptake, we traced the concept’s evolution in Scotland through a discourse analysis of 14 interviews, supplemented by key documents and events. Natural capital entered the Scottish context in the early 2010s, intended to make nature visible to decision-makers through economically valuing the environment. By the 2020s, concerns over insufficient public funding for ecological restoration, conceptualised as a nature finance gap, shifted focus to making nature financeable by the private sector. Subsequently, natural capital became emblematic of emergent nature markets, particularly carbon-based mechanisms, precipitating a boom in interest. As the risks of operationalising these markets became apparent to investors, confidence in natural capital faltered by 2023. This prompted the public sector to assume responsibility for de-risking market development. We argue natural capital has facilitated a discursive slide from advocacy for valuation towards practices of commodification, framing environmental crises as apolitical market opportunities. This trajectory tends towards privatisation of potential returns while socialising risk through public mechanisms. While natural capital may enhance aspects of nature’s legibility within existing political and economic systems, we caution that its discursive dominance constrains more transformative ambitions to reconfigure the structures that harm nature and its restoration.

title: Capping The Market: NIL Income Limits And The Shadow Of Antitrust Law
affiliations: University of Oregon - School of Law

detail.title: Capping The Market: NIL Income Limits And The Shadow Of Antitrust Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in Volume 64 of the Houston Law Review (2027)

detail.abstract:
This article addresses the newly created College Sports Commission (CSC) and its NIL clearinghouse, NIL Go. Currently, the collegiate sports industry is attempting to provide a workable framework to allow for limited athlete compensation via NIL while still imposing rules on the operation of college athletics. As part of the historic House settlement agreement in 2025, collegiate sports have implemented institutional NIL with a professional-style salary cap while simultaneously adopting limits on third-party income for college athletes. This article argues that both approaches will face significant hurdles under U.S. antitrust law. The NCAA and CSC, acting on behalf of market monopsonists, have jointly adopted restrictions on earnings that would result in per se violations of U.S. antitrust in any other private industry. However, even under the more lenient rule of reason approach, the collegiate athletics industry should be concerned over the viability of the new income caps.

Part I will briefly address the economic environment the college sports industry finds itself in (rising revenues and, in some cases, more quickly rising expenses) and its past issues attempting to curtail costs via its rulemaking authority. Part II of the article addresses the new, direct compensation model that allows universities to directly compensate athletes and examines the soundness of the model both as it pertains to direct university compensation as well as how it may relate to third-party NIL compensation. Part III addresses the new CSC and its clearinghouse, NIL Go, and examines the CSC’s standards by which NIL Go assesses the validity of third-party NIL deals and the difference in treatment for institutional NIL, collective-driven NIL and more traditional NIL opportunities. Part IV analyzes these new rules under traditional antitrust standards examining several recent cases challenging NCAA rules. This part concludes that, while college sports may desire greater policing powers, especially with third-party NIL, the current structure is unsustainable on legal grounds due to likely antitrust violations and practical issues of enforcement and compliance. The article concludes that, barring a new framework that allows for collective bargaining or the adoption of new legislation, college sports will continue to find themselves spending beyond the limits of the current rules and facing continued legal challenges to any enforcement activity.

title: Social and labour policy in a degrowth transition
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and Autonomous University of Barcelona

detail.title: Social and labour policy in a degrowth transition
detail.abstract: Degrowth promises to scale down damaging sectors of the economy while increasing human wellbeing. An unanswered question in the field regards how to prevent unemployment, create jobs, and reduce social deprivation in this transition. Here, we argue that a complementary package of social and labour policies displays high potential for resolving these problems. The package comprises a Public Job Guarantee, Universal Public Services, and a Universal Care Income. We employ the sustainable welfare criteria developed by Büchs (2021) to assess each policy’s effects in terms of 1) needs satisfaction, 2) planetary boundaries, 3) fair distribution, and 4) democratic governance. Deploying the critical method outlined by Eckersley (2021), we argue for the inclusion of a fifth criteria: political potential. This assessment highlights how considering these policies in the context of a degrowth transition requires increasing the ambition of each beyond its conceptualisation in the existing literature. We discuss the impact of the package on the necessary transformation of work in line with its contribution to social and ecological unsustainability. We conclude that the package has the potential to address key contradictions of the current conjuncture across societies in the global North ranging from the erosion of welfare systems to the rise of the far right.

title: The SbS Package and the Irony of Global Tax Cooperation

detail.title: The SbS Package and the Irony of Global Tax Cooperation
detail.abstract: On 5 January 2026, the OECD Inclusive Framework announced what many have heralded as a breakthrough: the Side-by-Side (SbS) Package. The package was presented as evidence of the maturity and adaptability of the global minimum tax (GMT) framework.Yet, paradoxically, it may have created precisely the opposite effect it intended—a powerful incentive structure for developing countries to strategically opt out of the GMT system through selective adoption of either the Income Inclusion Rule (IIR) or the Undertaxed Profit Rule (UTPR), while entirely forgoing the Qualified Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (QDMTT). The SbS regime, by designating only the United States as a “Qualified SbS Regime”, has inadvertently demonstrated a fundamental truth about global tax cooperation: when the rules systematically advantage one or only a few jurisdictions over others, the rational response for those excluded is not grateful compliance, but strategic withdrawal. This article argues that while developing countries may keep endorsing the GMT after the SbS package, they may opt for a more economically coherent strategy: selective defection. This outcome responds to two principal factors. First, the uncertain value of a QDMTT in the current scenario. Second, the strategic incentives offered by the SbS regime.

title: A Framework for Business Interruption Risk Modeling in Polymetallic Nodule Deep Sea Mining
affiliations: Arizona State University, CSIRO Mineral Resources, University of Arizona, Arizona State University (ASU) - School of Mathematical and Statistical Sciences and Arizona State University (ASU) - School of Mathematical and Statistical Sciences

detail.title: A Framework for Business Interruption Risk Modeling in Polymetallic Nodule Deep Sea Mining
detail.abstract: Deep-sea polymetallic nodule (PMN) mining is emerging as a potential source of critical minerals for global energy and technology supply chains. Yet it operates under extreme environmental uncertainty and limited operational experience, exposing projects to substantial business interruption (BI) risk. This paper develops a probabilistic and economically interpretable framework for modeling aggregate BI loss distributions in PMN mining under data-scarce conditions. To our knowledge, no existing study provides a system-level actuarial loss model for PMN mining that integrates causal dependency, restoration dynamics, and economic valuation. The proposed approach combines a Bayesian Belief Network (BBN) with expert-elicited conditional probabilities. Results show that interruption probability ranges from 19.3% under favorable conditions to 77% under adverse regimes. Sensitivity analysis identifies the basic control system, structural integrity, buoyancy system, mining plan, and emergency response as dominant contributors to interruption probability. However, cost-based analysis reveals that the highest BI losses are driven by a smaller subset of technical components. For single interruptions, expected restoration times range from 17.5 ± 3.8 days to 52.7 ± 20.4 days. However, multiple interruptions may occur randomly within a year. Accounting for these conditions, insurance pricing for annual premiums supporting system recovery can vary from $1.1 M to $10.9 M.

title: Ecological Characterization and Efficacy of Indigenous Entomopathogenic Nematodes Against Spodoptera frugiperda in Nigeria
affiliations: University of Bonn, University of Ibadan, University of Bonn and University of Bonn - Center for Development Research (ZEF)

detail.title: Ecological Characterization and Efficacy of Indigenous Entomopathogenic Nematodes Against Spodoptera frugiperda in Nigeria
detail.abstract: The successful deployment of entomopathogenic nematodes (EPNs) in biological pest control hinges on their ecological fitness and stress tolerance. In this study, we assessed the ecological traits and efficacy of six indigenous EPN isolates previously identified from distinct agroecological zones in Nigeria, targeting the invasive pest Spodoptera frugiperda (fall armyworm, FAW). The isolates, identified as Heterorhabditis bacteriophora (Ib-CRIN68), Steinernema carpocapsae (Ib-IART45, Ib-ITUC102), Steinernema feltiae (Za-SAM), Steinernema nepalense (Ib-HORT), and Oscheius myriophilus (Ib-FRIN32), were subjected to a series of ecological bioassays to evaluate their performance under temperature variation, moisture stress, oxygen limitation, oxidative stress, and foraging conditions. Results revealed significant inter- and intra-isolate variability in ecological tolerance traits. Optimal infectivity and reproduction were recorded between 25–30 °C, while mortality sharply declined at 10 °C and 35 °C. Foraging ability varied across substrates and soil depths, with S. carpocapsae isolates exhibiting strong host-finding capability under dry and surface conditions. Desiccation and oxidative stress assays also demonstrated the superior resilience of S. carpocapsae isolates, which sustained low mortality under Polyethylenglycol induced water stress and H2O2 exposure. Hypoxia assays indicated that all isolates were moderately tolerant to short-term anoxia, but only H. bacteriophora and the S. carpocapsae isolates survived above 50% at 72 h. Our study highlights the relevance of ecological screening as a prerequisite for selecting robust EPN candidate species and isolates suitable for biological control under variable conditions. The findings support the integration of indigenous EPNs into sustainable pest management frameworks in sub-Saharan Africa.

title: System-Critical Sectors for Decarbonisation and Mineral Security: An input-output study of Australian emissions
affiliations: University of Queensland - Center for Social Responsibility in Mining

detail.title: System-Critical Sectors for Decarbonisation and Mineral Security: An input-output study of Australian emissions
detail.abstract: This study examines the structure and transmission of embodied greenhouse gas emissions in the Australian economy over the 2007/08–2022/23 period using an integrated input-output framework. It combines emissions multiplier analysis with partial hypothetical extraction method (PHEM) to identify system-critical sectors and quantify upstream (supplier-side) and downstream (consumer-side) emissions reduction potentials. Emissions multiplier analysis reveals that electricity supply, agriculture, coal and oil and gas extraction, basic metals, and related manufacturing sectors exhibit strong upstream and downstream linkages, acting as central hubs for emissions propagation across the economy. PHEM results demonstrate that emissions reductions are highly non-linear and asymmetric across sectors. Electricity supply accounts for around two-thirds of total upstream and downstream emissions reduction potential when the inputs or outputs of nine focal sectors are partially extracted, while agriculture and heavy industry act as secondary transmission channels. Approximately 86% of total emissions reductions are captured by this small group of sectors, indicating a high degree of structural concentration. Historical trends further show uneven decarbonisation progress, with substantial emissions-intensity reductions in agriculture and selected manufacturing activities, but persistent rigidity in fossil-fuel extraction and transport. Based on these results, the study demonstrates the value of integrating mineral security with industrial policy to achieve dual objectives of decarbonisation and human development through target economic sectors.

title: Just transition or digital deadlock? Exploring the work-ecology nexus in Italy’s agrarian twin transition
affiliations: University of Pisa Department of Veterinary Sciences, University of Calabria and University of Bologna

detail.title: Just transition or digital deadlock? Exploring the work-ecology nexus in Italy’s agrarian twin transition
detail.abstract: The narrative on twin transition (green-digital) links digitalisation and decarbonisation as mutually reinforcing processes. In accordance to it the digital transformation of agriculture is framed as an inevitable step to increase efficiency, productivity, and sustainability. This article seeks to examining how the work-ecology nexus in agriculture is being reshaped under the twin transition agenda, and whether these transformations can be aligned with the principles of a just transition. The research addresses the question: how, and to what extent, does the twin transition redefine the relationships between production, work, and ecology in the agrarian sector? Empirically, the article examines two emblematic productions of Made in Italy, viticulture in Tuscany and industrial tomato production in Apulia. The research findings show how digitalisation operates as a selective socio-technical fix strategy for adaptation to multiple crises - labour shortages, social reproduction, and ecological stress the dominant narrative of the twin transition as an inherently sustainable and inclusive process - rather than as a driver of systemic transformation. It concentrates decision-making power and technical control among skilled actors, while reproducing inequalities between farms and reinforcing hierarchical divisions of labour, and without enabling deep agroecological transformations. In conclusion, the article highlights persistent gaps in the governance of ecological transition in Europe, by challenging the dominant narrative of the twin transition as an inherently sustainable and inclusive process.

title: Modeling nature land dynamics under distinct economic incentives: A stakeholder-driven simulation approach
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Eindhoven University of Technology (TUE) and Eindhoven University of Technology (TUE)

detail.title: Modeling nature land dynamics under distinct economic incentives: A stakeholder-driven simulation approach
detail.abstract: In densely populated and economically active regions, nature conservation is facing increasing pressure from competing demands for land use. While publicly financed subsidies are a critical policy tool to incentivize conservation, existing studies often overlook how different subsidy allocations between public stakeholders (e.g., municipal governments) and private stakeholders (e.g., nature managers) influence their behavior, interactions, and ultimately, conservation outcomes. This study addresses this gap by applying a spatially explicit land-use simulation model that integrates stakeholder interactions to assess how different subsidy allocations affect nature land protection in the Randstad, Netherlands.Three scenarios were developed to represent distinct subsidy arrangements between public and private stakeholders: (1) subsidies fully allocated to nature managers, (2) subsidies fully allocated to municipal governments, and (3) equal distribution to both stakeholders. Results show that incorporating stakeholder interactions significantly improves land-use modeling accuracy. Moreover, incorporating stakeholder interactions allows the model to capture potential spatial variations in conservation preferences among stakeholders under different subsidy allocations. These conflicts largely shape the different spatial patterns of nature land gains and losses across the region.The results highlight the importance of region-specific and goal-oriented strategies. In vulnerable nature areas facing intense urban or agriculture expansion, prioritizing subsidies to local nature managers is most effective in preventing fragmented nature loss. Conversely, in areas with high ecological potential near existing nature land, supporting municipal governments facilitates large-scale nature restoration. These findings highlight the critical role of aligning economic incentives with stakeholder roles and preferences to resolve conflicts and enhance the effectiveness of nature conservation policies.

detail.abstract: This chapter addresses a frequently overlooked retirement expense – the cost of nonmedical custodial care. Most individuals aged sixty-ﬁve or older will require Long-Term Care (LTC), also known as Long-Term Services and Supports. LTC includes assistance with activities of daily living (ADLs), such as eating, bathing, dressing, getting in and out of a chair, walking, toileting, and continence; and instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs), such as grocery shopping, banking, bill paying, and ﬁlling prescriptions. Most LTC is unpaid family care because paid LTC is very expensive. For example, the average annual cost of LTC is about $100,000 for a room in a nursing home and about $60,000 for 40 hours per week of in-home care. Access to paid LTC currently is a patchwork crazy quilt of public (federal, state, and local) and private funding mechanisms. Medicare generally does not cover LTC, although many people assume it does. State-run Medicaid programs provide signiﬁcant LTC funding – but only to Medicaid-eligible persons with low income and almost no savings. This chapter ﬁrst explores the implications – for current and future seniors and their caregivers – of increased longevity and other trends on unpaid family LTC and on publicly funded and privately funded paid LTC. Second, this chapter surveys alternative means of accessing and funding LTC. Third, this chapter notes LTC trends, innovations, legal developments, and proposals that might improve the LTC outlook for seniors and their families.

title: Are the Big Ten and SEC Monopoly PROs? Publicity Rights Organizations and New NIL Antitrust Questions
affiliations: University of Illinois College of Law

detail.title: Are the Big Ten and SEC Monopoly PROs? Publicity Rights Organizations and New NIL Antitrust Questions

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Illinois College of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Illinois College of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: The Big Ten and SEC NIL form contracts pose new antitrust concerns for athletes. This Article develops a blueprint for athletes to sue under the Sherman Act to protect them from misappropriation, misrepresentation, and falsification of their NIL under the Lanham Act; illegal antitrust immunity; and unjust enrichment. Schools and conferences act as PROs— publicity rights organizations— by purchasing, licensing, and selling athlete NIL rights. My antitrust analysis compares the Big Ten and SEC to BMI, Inc., a music industry marketer used by composers and performers to sell copyrighted music to radio and TV broadcasters. BMI, Inc. avoids antitrust liability by contracting for music rights with ASCAP, a group formed by music creators. In contrast, the Big Ten and SEC NIL contracts do not involve an entity that represents athletes. The contracts eliminate competition between schools for purchasing and marketing NIL rights. College athletes are barred by contract from receiving continuing royalties, unlike music creators who license their work through ASCAP and sell licenses through BMI, Inc. This is horizontal price fixing, removing competition in the NIL marketplace between schools, because NIL contracts uniformly set royalties at $0. Big Ten and SEC price fixing prevents competition between School A, which could offer $1 million in a one-time NIL payment while avoiding any royalty payments, and School B, which could offer $900,000 in an NIL payment with a guarantee to pay the athlete 20% of net-profit royalties in perpetuity on sales of his NIL (e.g., jersey with his number and name).

title: AI innovation and firm-level employment: Evidence from the EU energy sector
affiliations: University of Southampton, University of Southampton, University of Southampton and Tsinghua University

detail.title: AI innovation and firm-level employment: Evidence from the EU energy sector
detail.abstract: The concurrent digital and green transitions are reshaping the European energy landscape, with artificial intelligence (AI) serving as a critical yet underexplored force. This paper investigates the effects of AI innovation on employment and wages within the European Union (EU) energy sector from 2014 to 2023. Combining firm-level financial data with AI patent metrics, we construct a dataset of 315 EU energy firms (214 traditional energy firms and 101 renewable energy firms) across 27 EU countries. We find that AI innovation significantly reduces overall employment. The negative employment impact is significantly stronger in the renewable energy sector, suggesting that the capital-intensive, data-rich, and rapidly scaling nature of green technologies presents a context ripe for labor-displacing automation. Conversely, we find a slightly positive effect of AI on average wages. Importantly, we identify a bidirectional relationship: past employment levels positively predict subsequent AI innovation, indicating that workforce capacity or costs foster technological invention. Our findings highlight an unequal distribution of transition costs, where the green transition's frontline sectors face heightened digital disruption. We conclude that integrated "twin transition" policies - combining targeted reskilling for vulnerable workforce segments in renewables and proactive social safety nets - are urgently needed to ensure an equitable and publicly sustainable path to decarbonization.

title: How Competitive Is Renewable Hydrogen? A Scenario-Based Techno-Economic Assessment for Western Australia
affiliations: Curtin University, Curtin University, DBP, Curtin University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: How Competitive Is Renewable Hydrogen? A Scenario-Based Techno-Economic Assessment for Western Australia
detail.abstract: Green hydrogen is considered a key pathway for decarbonising energy systems, yet adoption is hindered by high production costs and infrastructure constraints. This study conducts a comprehensive techno-economic assessment of large-scale hydrogen production in Western Australia across three operational configurations that map to two distinct cost regimes: grid-connected electrolysis exposed to wholesale electricity prices (Scenarios A and B), and renewable-only electrolysis supplied by co-located wind–solar generation under a long-term power purchase agreement (PPA) cost structure (Scenario C). Using real five-minute wholesale prices, Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA)–based renewable profiles, and size-scaling of proton exchange membrane (PEM) and alkaline electrolysers from 5–100 MW, we quantify how utilisation, renewable variability, capital expenditure (CAPEX) learning, and policy incentives shape the levelised cost of hydrogen (LCOH, AUD kg−1 H2). Grid-connected configurations (Scenarios A and B) benefit from higher utilisation and the ability to concentrate operation in low-price intervals, with LCOH decreasing to 6.1 AUD kg−1 (Scenario A) and 7.3 AUD kg−1 (Scenario B) at 100 MW, while acting as a flexible source of electricity demand that absorbs surplus generation and reduces curtailment risk. However, these outcomes remain bounded by a price-based cost floor imposed by electricity market conditions and system tightness. In contrast, the renewable-only configuration (Scenario C) is structurally constrained by wind–solar variability and minimum operating loads, yielding higher baseline costs at small scale; nevertheless, its electricity cost is largely capital- and financing-driven under long-term contracting. Under Scenario C, LCOH falls from 19.3 to 7.0 AUD kg−1 (PEM) and 14.5 to 5.8 AUD kg−1 (alkaline) between 5 and 100 MW. Stacked credits for carbon abatement and oxygen co-production reduce Scenario C costs uniformly by approximately 0.56 AUD kg−1, yielding net LCOH values of 6.47 AUD kg−1 (PEM) and 5.26 AUD kg−1 (alkaline) at 100 MW. On a higher-heating-value basis, these correspond to approximately 46 and 37 AUD GJ−1, remaining well above Western Australia’s industrial methane price band (8-12 AUD GJ−1). The results demonstrate that hydrogen competitiveness is state-contingent rather than technology-determined: electricity market structure favours grid-connected hydrogen when surplus electricity exists, whereas renewable-only hydrogen becomes relatively more attractive under electricity scarcity or low-cost finance. These findings highlight the central role of electricity market design, contracting structures, and targeted policy incentives in shaping hydrogen deployment pathways in high-renewable power systems.

title: SMEs, Complex Systems, and Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: Reconceptualizing Expertise as a Dynamic Computational Layer

detail.title: SMEs, Complex Systems, and Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: Reconceptualizing Expertise as a Dynamic Computational Layer

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly deployed across healthcare systems with the promise of enhancing prediction, efficiency, and decision support. Yet many AI implementations underperform not because of technical limitations, but because they misunderstand the cognitive role of human expertise in complex environments. This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework that positions Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) not as repositories of domain knowledge, but as dynamic computational agents embedded within complex healthcare systems. Drawing from complexity science, distributed cognition, and health informatics practice, the analysis argues that SMEs continuously perform real-time system modeling that artificial intelligence cannot independently replicate. Rather than replacing expertise, AI should be designed to augment and extend this human computational function. This reconceptualization has significant implications for AI design, governance, informatics leadership, and organizational decision-making. By reframing expertise as a computational layer within healthcare decision ecosystems, this paper offers a new foundation for integrating AI into environments characterized by uncertainty, interdependence, and continuous adaptation.

title: Income Fluctuations and Life Satisfaction: A Gain-Loss Asymmetry Perspective Evidence from the German Socio-Economic Panel
affiliations: Tekirdag Namik Kemal University and Marmara University

detail.title: Income Fluctuations and Life Satisfaction: A Gain-Loss Asymmetry Perspective Evidence from the German Socio-Economic Panel
detail.abstract: The primary aim of this paper is to explore the impact of real-life income fluctuations on individuals, focusing specifically on "gain-loss asymmetry"-a phenomenon where losses exert a more pronounced psychological effect than equivalent gains. By analyzing data from the German SocioEconomic Panel (SOEP), this study evaluates the effects of actual income changes on experienced utility, distinguishing between real income variations and anticipated changes. Self-reported life satisfaction is used as a proxy for experienced utility, with income changes determined by comparing current net real household income to that of the previous five years. Employing an ordinary least squares model with a two-way fixed effect estimator, our findings reveal that income losses significantly and negatively affect life satisfaction compared to equivalent gains, with the exception of the first lag. Beyond the first lag, losses exert a significantly greater impact than gains. Notably, the gain-loss asymmetry is more pronounced among middle-income individuals, while categorical losses are more impactful for higher-income groups.

title: E-Banking: Technological Advancement, Challenges and Opportunities in the Digital Economy

detail.title: E-Banking: Technological Advancement, Challenges and Opportunities in the Digital Economy
detail.abstract:
A change in the banking system to electronic banking (e-banking) has been one of the discontinuities to the financial sector to substitute the traditional banking system that was in operation through branches. E-banking is an offering of banking products and services through digital products such as mobile applications, web-based banking, and electronic wallets and it allows banking clients to conduct banking transactions at a place
and any time. This fact of technological change has not only made operations more efficient and even more convenient to the customers, but it has also revolutionized the competitive scene in the global financial world. The chapter is also critical examination of the transformational aspect of e-banking in terms of technology base, benefits, and emergent trends. It also cites the impact of technological advances such as artificial intelligence, blockchain, cloud computing, and cybersecurity models to transform financial services. On the way, the chapter encounters the following current issues: privacy of data, fraud, digital divide and compliance with regulatory statutes.After discussing the opportunities and threats, in this chapter, e-banking is presented as a two-sided phenomenon that can bring about financial inclusiveness and corporal growth,
on the one hand, and governance, ethical, and policy issues, on the other hand. It is founded upon the international practice and experience that relies on the case studies to highlight the significance of resilient, transparent, and inclusive e-banking systems that can be sustained to maintain the confidence to the digital transformation of the corporate world and corporate world over the long term.

title: Applying Machine Learning Data Imputation Techniques for Missing Data in the Analysis of Financial Development and Trade Openness in Africa: Evidence From CFA Countries
affiliations: Eastern Mediterranean University

detail.title: Applying Machine Learning Data Imputation Techniques for Missing Data in the Analysis of Financial Development and Trade Openness in Africa: Evidence From CFA Countries

keywords: Missing Data Imputation Techniques in Statistical Analysis

detail.abstract: This study addresses the critical challenge of missingness in African macroeconomic data, by employing advanced machine learning imputation to enhance the reliability of economic analysis. Utilizing panel data from 13 Communauté Financière Africaine (CFA) countries spanning 1980-2023, the research tackles a 2.5% missingness rate through a hybrid supervised-unsupervised learning framework. The methodology first applies K-means clustering to group data into optimal homogenous subsets, followed by the k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) algorithm for precise imputation. The accuracy of this approach is validated by low Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) scores. Econometric analysis was then conducted using the Feasible Generalized Least Square (FGLS) Methodology, which is robust to the detected cross-sectional dependence, heteroskedasticity, and autocorrelation in the panel data. The main findings demonstrate a positive and statistically significant relationship between financial development, trade openness, and economic growth. Crucially, the analysis of the interaction term between financial development and trade openness revealed a negative coefficient. This suggests that insufficient financial development acts as a moderator, diminishing the positive impact of trade openness on economic development in the CFA region. In conclusion, the study successfully illustrates the value of machine learning in producing more reliable economic insights and highlights the necessity of strengthening financial systems to fully capitalize on the benefits of trade liberalization in Africa.
